name: Frankincense gum wrinkle remedy

lead: This entry covers a traditional remedy attributed to ancient Egypt in which frankincense gum, often combined with moringa, is applied to the face with the aim of reducing the look of wrinkles.
Frankincense is the aromatic resin of Boswellia trees. The Ebers Papyrus (c. 1500 BCE) is cited as some of the earliest evidence of deliberate therapeutic use of frankincense.

paras: Practitioners of home and natural-skincare traditions describe applying a resin-based preparation to facial skin. Details of preparation vary between accounts.
Plant resins and oils can cause allergic or irritant reactions in some people. No clinical trial has tested this specific remedy.

chain: Resin-based preparation applied to the face
Believed to soften and tone the skin
angle.text: Proponents apply frankincense-based preparations to the face with the aim of reducing the look of fine lines. This is a traditional claim; no clinical study of this specific recipe is known.

lead: The frankincense and moringa wrinkle remedy is a traditional preparation attributed to ancient Egypt, in which frankincense resin is applied to the skin in the hope of a smoother, younger-looking complexion. It circulates in natural-skincare circles as a historical beauty recipe.

Frankincense is the resin of Boswellia trees, and Egyptians traded for incense from the land of Punt from at least the third millennium BCE.[1] The Ebers Papyrus, dated to about 1500 BCE, provides some of the earliest evidence of frankincense used with intent as a possible therapy.[1] Wikipedia notes that research on frankincense for health conditions remains limited and inconclusive.[1]

paras: Frankincense was valued in ancient Egypt as incense, and the Ebers Papyrus records it among early therapeutic ingredients.[1] The attribution of a specific wrinkle-reducing recipe to Egyptian beauty practice is a popular claim in natural-skincare writing; the sources consulted do not document its exact historical form.
Modern accounts describe applying the resin or a preparation of it, sometimes with moringa, to the face. Preparation methods vary and are not standardised.
No studies found. General research on frankincense (Boswellia) for health conditions is limited and described as inconclusive.[1]

timeline.event: Ebers Papyrus records early therapeutic use of frankincense.[1]
